chunks: "An ideal dielectric just stores energy: the field polarizes it, and when the field reverses you get that energy back.
Real dielectrics turn some of it into heat, and there are a few ways that happens. The first is plain conduction.
No insulator is perfect, so a tiny leakage current flows and you get I to the 2R loss. That dominates at DC and low frequency. The bigger one at AC is polarization loss.
When you apply a field, polar molecules rotate, ions shift and electron clouds distort.
If the field alternates, those charges have to keep reorienting, and they can't follow instantly.
They lag behind the field and lose energy to friction with neighbouring molecules, which shows up as heat.
The loss peaks when the frequency is around one over the material's relaxation time. A microwave oven heats water exactly this way.
In high-κ ceramics like X7R there's also hysteresis from ferroelectric domains switching, and at high voltage you can get partial discharge in tiny voids.
We quantify all of it with the loss tangent, delta .

Dissipated power is V squared omega C delta , so it matters for capacitors with large AC voltage and for PCB laminates at gigahertz, which is why you'd pick C0G or film caps, and low-loss laminates for high-speed links."
